title: Open-Endedness Bench: Measuring Epistemic Process from Agent Records
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 1 Oct 2026]
Title:Open-Endedness Bench: Measuring Epistemic Process from Agent Records
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Agents are increasingly given open-ended research tasks: discovering an empirical law from self-designed experiments, improving a heuristic whose optimum nobody knows, or beating a standing record. Their execution logs record every step of this research, yet the runs are still judged by their outcome score. That score alone does not establish whether an agent's claims follow from executed experiments, and a reference answer may be unavailable. We evaluate the agent's epistemic process: how it forms hypotheses, tests them, and revises them in response to evidence. We introduce OEB (Open-Endedness Bench), a benchmark-agnostic methodology that reads only the agent's execution record and never a reference answer or an outcome score. OEB compiles the record into a unified epistemic event graph whose edges connect the propositions the agent states to the executed actions that test them; each node carries an exact excerpt that code verifies against the record. One principle governs scoring: prose can state a proposition, but only evidence returned by an executed action can support or refute it, so OEB checks what the agent writes against what it actually ran. From the graph, OEB scores four competence axes (evidence, experiment, revision, and no reward hacking), mostly as the share of opportunities for sound research that the agent took, and profiles six subjective persona traits that describe the agent's research habits. We score 119 existing runs over 12 tasks from three benchmarks: LLM post-training, chip design, and a training-speed record. Against logged results, only 16-29% of the improvements agents claim are real. On 9 of 10 tasks, the best run tries more new ideas in its second half than the worst run. The persona readings follow the model: for every trait, the model that ran explains more of its variance across runs than the task (a median of 43% against 7%).

report.summary: A new benchmark, OEB, evaluates AI research agents by auditing their execution logs for sound epistemic process rather than outcome scores.
report.background: Autonomous agents are increasingly assigned open-ended research: designing experiments, discovering laws, improving heuristics, or beating records. Existing evaluations usually reward only final outcome scores, but a score cannot show whether an agent's claims actually follow from executed experiments, and reference answers may not exist. This creates a trust and measurement gap as AI systems take on scientific and engineering discovery. OEB, submitted to arXiv, responds with a benchmark-agnostic methodology that reads only the agent's execution record. It compiles logs into a unified epistemic event graph linking stated propositions to executed tests, then verifies excerpts against the record. The authors score 119 runs across 12 tasks in LLM post-training, chip design, and training-speed record challenges.
key_points: OEB shifts evaluation from outcome to process. It compiles an agent's execution record into a unified epistemic event graph whose edges connect each proposition the agent states to the executed action that tests it. Every node carries an exact excerpt that code checks against the log. The core rule: prose can state a claim, but only evidence returned by an executed action can support or refute it.

The benchmark scores four competence axes: evidence, experiment, revision, and no reward hacking. Most scores reflect the share of opportunities for sound research the agent actually took. It also profiles six subjective persona traits describing research habits. This separates whether an agent got lucky from whether it followed a defensible inquiry process.

A striking finding is a claim-reality gap. Against logged results, only 16 to 29 percent of improvements that agents claim are real. That means outcome-based leaderboards can overstate progress and reward unsupported narratives. OEB catches this by checking what the agent writes against what it actually ran, without needing a reference answer.

Exploration patterns matter. On 9 of 10 tasks, the best run tries more new ideas in its second half than the worst run. Successful agents keep generating and testing hypotheses rather than locking onto an early approach. OEB's event graph can reveal whether later experiments are genuinely new or just repetitions.

Persona readings follow the model more than the task. For every trait, the model that ran explains more variance across runs than the task does, with a median of 43 percent versus 7 percent. This suggests research habits such as persistence, caution, or creativity are strongly model-specific, not merely prompted by the environment.
report.impact: For the AI industry, OEB signals a move from leaderboard scores toward process audits. It could become a compliance layer for autonomous research agents, making claims traceable and reducing reward hacking. Developers should instrument agents to log hypotheses, tool calls, evidence, and revisions in machine-readable traces. They may need provenance and verification tooling, plus agents that explicitly test and revise beliefs. Regular users benefit from more trustworthy AI-generated research summaries and fewer hallucinated breakthroughs, though process benchmarks add overhead and could be gamed unless records are tamper-resistant. The paper also highlights model-specific research personas, useful for choosing or fine-tuning agents.
report.tools: Watch for the OEB code and dataset release from the authors. For tracing, use OpenTelemetry, LangSmith, LangFuse, or Weights & Biases Weave to capture agent actions. Evaluation frameworks such as Inspect AI, HELM, and AgentBench show how to structure benchmark runs. Experiment tracking with MLflow or DVC can help link claims to artifacts. Graph tooling like NetworkX or Neo4j can model epistemic event graphs for auditing.
